candidates.title: Pericapsular Nerve Group Block Significantly Reduces Morphine Consumption and Improves Early Recovery Following Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty: A Randomized Double-Blind Sham-Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Demirkıran F, Özdemir Kol İ, Altun O
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The pericapsular nerve group (PENG) block has emerged as a promising regional analgesic technique for hip surgery. However, evidence regarding its opioid-sparing efficacy following primary total hip arthroplasty remains limited. This study evaluated the effect of ultrasound-guided PENG block on postoperative opioid consumption, pain scores, and recovery outcomes following primary total hip arthroplasty. METHODS: In this prospective, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 40 patients undergoing elective primary total hip arthroplasty under general anesthesia were randomized to receive either ultrasound-guided PENG block with one mg/kg bupivacaine diluted to 30 mL (n = 20) or a sham procedure with 30 mL saline (n = 20). The primary outcome was cumulative morphine consumption during the first 24 postoperative hours. The secondary outcomes included visual analog scale (VAS) pain scores, time to first rescue analgesia, patient satisfaction, and opioid-related adverse events. Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups. RESULTS: Cumulative morphine consumption was significantly lower in the PENG group throughout the postoperative period and at 24 hours (6.2 ± 3.3 versus 30.2 ± 5.6 mg, P < 0.001), representing an approximately 79% reduction in opioid requirement. The visual analog scale pain scores were significantly lower at all postoperative assessment points (all P < 0.001). Time to first rescue analgesic requirement was significantly prolonged in the PENG group (16.0 ± 0.0 versus 1.4 ± 0.5 hours, P < 0.001). Patient satisfaction was significantly greater in the PENG group (P < 0.001), while postoperative nausea occurred less frequently (zero versus 25%, P = 0.017). There were no block-related complications observed. CONCLUSIONS: Ultrasound-guided PENG block provided effective opioid-sparing analgesia following primary total hip arthroplasty, significantly reducing postoperative morphine consumption and pain scores while improving patient satisfaction and reducing postoperative nausea. These findings support the incorporation of PENG block into multimodal analgesic protocols for total hip arthroplasty.
candidates.score_reasoning: RCT design evaluating PENG block for THA with strong opioid-sparing results (79% reduction) published in a high-volume arthroplasty journal, directly applicable to perioperative pain management practice.
bullets: In adults undergoing primary total hip arthroplasty, a PENG block cut 24-hour morphine use by roughly 79% compared to sham injection (6 mg vs 30 mg).
Patients who received the PENG block went about 16 hours before needing rescue analgesia, versus under 2 hours in the control group.
For orthopaedic teams managing hip replacement, adding a PENG block to multimodal analgesia protocols meaningfully reduces opioid consumption and postoperative nausea without reported complications.

candidates.title: No Differences in Patient-reported Outcomes Between the Direct Anterior and Posterolateral Approach for THA: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Rykov K, de Vries AJ, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The direct anterior approach (DAA) for THA is seeing wider use because it is purported to deliver a faster postoperative recovery. However, most previous studies comparing the DAA with the posterolateral approach (PLA) were limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneous patient populations, and the use of outcome measures with ceiling effects. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: (1) Does the DAA result in a higher proportion of patients achieving the patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) on the Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (HOOS) after THA compared with the PLA? (2) Are there differences in symptoms, physical function, life activities and participation, health-related quality of life (QoL), or complications between the DAA and PLA in the first postoperative year? METHODS: A prospective, parallel-group, nonblinded, randomized controlled trial comparing the DAA and PLA for THA was conducted. Patients with primary or secondary osteoarthritis with an indication for THA with an uncemented femoral stem and cemented acetabular component were eligible. Of the 241 patients assessed for eligibility, 53% (128) were included in the study. Fifty-one percent (65 of 128) were randomized to the DAA group, and 49% (63 of 128) were randomized to the PLA group. One patient in each group was lost to follow-up, leaving 98% (64 of 65) and 98% (62 of 63) of patients available for analysis, respectively. There were no between-group differences in baseline or perioperative measurements. The primary outcome was achievement of the PASS on the HOOS at 3 months postoperatively. An a priori sample-size calculation indicated that 60 patients per group were required to detect a 20% difference in PASS achievement between groups (80% power; α = 0.05). With an expected loss to follow-up of 10%, the sample size was set to 65 patients per group. Secondary outcomes included symptoms, physical functioning, participation, and health-related QoL, assessed using patient-reported outcome measures and physical performance tests. Complications were assessed using the Clavien-Dindo classification. Outcomes were assessed preoperatively as well as at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, 3 months, and 1 year postoperatively. RESULTS: At 3 months, the proportion of patients achieving the PASS did not differ between the DAA and PLA for any HOOS subscales, including symptoms (65% [41 of 63] versus 63% [39 of 62], OR 1.03 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.80 to 1.35]; p = 0.80), pain (48% [30 of 63] versus 53% [33 of 62], OR 0.90 [95% CI 0.63 to 1.27]; p = 0.53), activities of daily living (68% [43 of 63] versus 65% [40 of 62], OR 1.06 [95% CI 0.82 to 1.36]; p = 0.66), sports and recreation (55% [34 of 62] versus 58% [36 of 62], OR 0.94 [95% CI 0.69 to 1.29]; p = 0.72), and QoL (73% [46 of 63] versus 71% [44 of 62], OR 1.03 [95% CI 0.83 to 1.28]; p = 0.80). There were no between-group differences in symptoms, physical function, life activities and participation, and health-related QoL at any time point. Complications occurred in 8% (5 of 65) of patients in the DAA group and 2% (1 of 63) of patients in the PLA group (OR 3.05 [95% CI 0.51 to 18.40]; p = 0.21). CONCLUSION: In this randomized controlled trial, the DAA did not improve patient-reported or functional outcomes compared with the PLA during the first postoperative year. In the absence of demonstrated patient-reported or functional benefits of the DAA, surgeons should not represent to patients that the DAA provides advantages in terms of the pace or magnitude of recovery. Future studies powered to detect differences in the risk of complications should be performed to see whether harms are more likely with the DAA than with other surgical approaches. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: RCT from CORR comparing DAA vs posterolateral approach for THA with robust methodology, adequate sample size, and clinically meaningful null finding that directly informs surgical approach selection.
bullets: In this RCT of 128 THA patients, the direct anterior approach produced no better pain, function, or quality of life scores than the posterolateral approach at any point through one year.
Patients undergoing primary or secondary hip OA treated with THA can expect equivalent recovery regardless of which of these two approaches their surgeon uses.
Surgeons should stop telling patients the anterior approach means a faster or greater recovery, as this trial finds no evidence to support that claim.

candidates.title: Total Hip Arthroplasty versus Hemiarthroplasty for Displaced Fragility Femoral Neck Fractures in Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Mortality, Reoperation, and Surgical Complications.
candidates.authors_short: Pierce TP, Badawi JM, et al.
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Femoral neck fractures in the elderly are managed surgically, most often with either a total hip arthroplasty (THA) or hemiarthroplasty. The purpose of this meta-analysis was to compare the risk of: (1) mortality; (2) revision; and (3) surgical complications of those who undergo THA or hemiarthroplasty for fragility femoral neck fractures. METHODS: A thorough review of four electronic databases (PubMed, CINAHL plus, EMBASE, and SCOPUS) was performed for all articles pertaining to this topic from 2016 to 2026. A total of 31 studies were included. Mortality was evaluated at 1-month and 1-year. All other surgical complications were stratified based on short-term (≤ two years) and long-term outcomes (greater than two years). The final cohort consisted of 114,064 THAs and 443,016 hemiarthroplasties. The THA cohort was younger (-0.62 years; P = 0.0001), and the hemiarthroplasty cohort had more women (74.1 versus 70.5%; P = 0.0001). RESULTS: A THA was associated with lower 1-year mortality (random relative risk (RR), 0.79; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.65 to 0.97; P = 0.02) without heterogeneity (P = 0.11; I2 = 40%) or publication bias (P = 0.77). The cohort undergoing THA had a higher risk of instability in long-term (random RR, 1.84; 95% CI, 1.66 to 2.04; P = 0.0001) without heterogeneity (P = 0.41; I2 = 2%) or publication bias (P = 0.31). DISCUSSION: Those who undergo THA for fragility femoral neck fractures may have a decreased risk of 1-year mortality while having an increased risk of postoperative instability. Our study was unable to determine a difference in the risk of 1-month mortality, revision, periprosthetic joint infection, and periprosthetic fractures between the cohorts. Future studies should evaluate the role of surgery- and patient-specific variables in outcomes following hemiarthroplasty and THA for femoral neck fracture.
candidates.score_reasoning: Meta-analysis on THA vs hemiarthroplasty for fragility femoral neck fractures with large cohort (557,080 patients) showing THA associated with lower 1-year mortality, directly impacting one of the most common orthopaedic decisions.
bullets: In elderly patients with displaced femoral neck fractures, total hip arthroplasty was associated with lower one-year mortality compared to hemiarthroplasty.
Patients who received total hip arthroplasty had nearly twice the risk of dislocation over the long term compared to those who received hemiarthroplasty.
For older adults with femoral neck fractures, the choice between total hip arthroplasty and hemiarthroplasty involves a tradeoff between survival benefit and increased dislocation risk.

candidates.title: Tranexamic Acid Administration is Associated With Lower Transfusion Rates and Wound Complications Following Revision Total Knee Arthroplasty for Periprosthetic Joint Infection.
candidates.authors_short: Kumaran P, Wier J, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tranexamic acid (TXA) is widely used in total joint arthroplasty, but data on its efficacy in periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) of the knee are scarce. We assessed TXA efficacy in revision total knee arthroplasty (TKA) for PJI. METHODS: A national database was queried for patients ≥18 years undergoing stage-one revision TKA for PJI from 2016 to 2023. Patients with and without TXA exposure were propensity matched. Multivariable logistic regression assessed primary outcomes (postoperative transfusion, bleeding complications, and wound complications) and secondary outcomes (thromboembolic complications). RESULTS: Overall, 13,247 TXA patients were matched 1:1 to 13,247 non-TXA patients on comorbidities, Charlson Comorbidity Index, demographics, hospital characteristics, and preoperative transfusion rates, all with standardized mean differences <0.10. Mean age was 67.4 years in both cohorts, with similar use of venous thromboembolic chemoprophylaxis. TXA was associated with decreased adjusted odds of postoperative transfusion (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]: 0.77, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.69-0.85, P < .001) and aggregate wound complications (aOR: 0.65, 95% CI: 0.60-0.70, P < .001), with similar odds of aggregate bleeding complications (aOR: 1.02, 95% CI: 0.95-1.09, P = .563). Odds of aggregate venous thromboembolism (aOR: 0.97, 95% CI: 0.82-1.13, P = .874), deep vein thrombosis (aOR: 1.00, 95% CI: 1.00-1.01, P = .309), and pulmonary embolism (aOR: 1.06, 95% CI: 0.83-1.34, P = .639) were similar. CONCLUSIONS: TXA was associated with lower rates of transfusion and aggregate wound complications, without increased venous thromboembolism risk, during revision TKA for PJI.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large propensity-matched database study (26,494 patients) showing TXA significantly reduces transfusion and wound complications in revision TKA for PJI, with immediately actionable findings for a high-risk patient population.
bullets: In over 26,000 matched patients undergoing first-stage revision knee arthroplasty for periprosthetic joint infection, TXA reduced transfusion rates and wound complications compared to no TXA.
TXA did not increase the risk of DVT, pulmonary embolism, or bleeding complications in this high-risk infection revision population.
Surgeons can use TXA in staged revision knee arthroplasty for periprosthetic joint infection without added clotting risk and with meaningful reductions in transfusion and wound complications.

candidates.title: Does the Timing of Surgical Debridement Affect Outcomes in Septic Arthritis of the Native Hip and Knee? A Propensity-weighted Analysis.
candidates.authors_short: Randall ZD, Barber HF, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Septic arthritis of the native hip and knee can cause irreversible cartilage damage and systemic illness. Because operative debridement provides source control, delaying it may permit infection to progress, potentially increasing the need for repeat surgery and the risk of death; however, evidence examining these associations remains limited. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: Is delayed debridement associated with increased risk of (1) repeat debridement or (2) 1-year mortality in septic arthritis of the native hip and/or knee? METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the Florida State Inpatient Database, a statewide, all-payer database that records procedures by hospital day and includes longitudinal patient identifiers. Between October 2015 and December 2022, we identified 3587 adult admissions involving septic arthritis of the native hip (n = 1014) or knee (n = 2573) treated with surgical debridement. We excluded 1% (42 of 3587) of admitted patients in whom the first debridement occurred after hospital day 10, leaving 99% (3545 of 3587) for analysis (hip n = 1001; knee n = 2544). No included outcome or covariate data were missing. In the screened hip and knee cohorts, the mean ± SD ages were 55 ± 17 years and 60 ± 16 years, respectively, and 46% (462 of 1014) and 34% (879 of 2573) were female. Debridement occurred on hospital days 0 to 1 in 51% (506 of 1001) of hip admissions and 59% (1510 of 2544) of knee admissions; the remaining 49% (495 of 1001) and 41% (1034 of 2544), respectively, underwent debridement on day 2 or later. Stabilized inverse probability-of-treatment weighting was used to balance measured baseline covariates. Weighted log-binomial regression was used to estimate adjusted relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). RESULTS: Among patients with septic knee arthritis, debridement on day 2 or later was associated with a higher risk of repeat debridement than debridement on days 0 to 1 (13% [133 of 1034] versus 5% [72 of 1510], adjusted RR 2.40 [95% CI 1.81 to 3.19]; p < 0.001). One-year mortality also was higher after debridement on day 2 or later (11% [118 of 1034] versus 6% [88 of 1510], adjusted RR 1.54 [95% CI 1.17 to 2.02]; p = 0.002). Among patients with septic hip arthritis, repeat debridement was no different between those treated on day 2 or later and those treated on days 0 to 1 (11% [55 of 495] versus 7% [37 of 506], adjusted RR 1.43 [95% CI 0.95 to 2.15]; p = 0.09). One-year mortality also was no different between the hip timing groups (9% [43 of 495] versus 7% [35 of 506], adjusted RR 1.19 [95% CI 0.77 to 1.85]; p = 0.44). CONCLUSION: Surgeons should prioritize prompt debridement of septic knee arthritis, and hospitals should implement coordinated pathways to avoid preventable delays. No timing-specific recommendation can be made for septic hip arthritis based on our findings. Larger multicenter studies with granular data on presentation, diagnostic aspiration, antibiotic administration, and debridement are needed to clarify whether debridement timing influences outcomes in septic hip arthritis and to distinguish preventable delays from those related to diagnostic uncertainty or the management of medical comorbidities. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: RCT comparing CR vs PS robotic TKA gap balancing in 120 patients with 2-year follow-up, directly informing implant selection decisions in the growing robotic-assisted TKA space.
bullets: In septic knee arthritis, delaying surgical debridement to day 2 or later more than doubled the risk of repeat surgery and increased one-year mortality by 54% compared to debridement within the first day.
For septic hip arthritis, debridement timing did not significantly affect repeat surgery rates or one-year mortality, so no firm timing recommendation can be made for the hip.
Orthopaedic surgeons should treat septic knee arthritis as a time-sensitive emergency and hospitals should build care pathways to prevent avoidable delays to the operating room.

candidates.title: Comparison of computed tomography-based tibial torsion measurement techniques reveals significant technique-dependent differences.
candidates.authors_short: Benefelds M, Juen U, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare commonly used computed tomography (CT)-based tibial torsion measurement discrepancies and evaluate their intra- and interobserver agreement, as measurement discrepancies between techniques have not been systematically assessed. METHODS: CT scans from 20 adult patients were retrospectively analysed. Tibial torsion was calculated using two proximal reference axes (posterior tibial plateau tangent and tibial tuberosity axis) and four distal axes (transmalleolar, ankle joint, Jend and Waidelich). Three observers performed all measurements independently and repeated them after 8-12 weeks. Differences among techniques were assessed using repeated-measures analysis of variance with Bonferroni correction. Reliability was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). RESULTS: All measurement techniques differed significantly (p < 0.05). Mean tibial torsion was 34.1° (standard deviation [SD] 8.6°) for the transmalleolar axis, 31.2° (SD 8.8°) for the ankle joint axis, 44.2° (SD 9.8°) for the Jend axis and 34.9° (SD 9.0°) for the Waidelich axis. Segmental values revealed a mean supratuberositary torsion of 26° (SD 6.7°) and a mean infratuberositary torsion of 7.9° (SD 8.8°) for the transmalleolar axis, 5.1° (SD 8.9°) for the ankle joint axis, 18.1° (SD 10.4°) for the Jend axis and 8.8° (SD 9.1°) for the Waidelich axis. All techniques showed excellent intra- and interobserver reliability (ICC > 0.89). CONCLUSION: Tibial torsion values depended strongly on the measurement technique used. Technique-specific normative values are essential, and radiology reports should explicitly identify the technique applied. Clinicians must account for these systematic differences when interpreting torsion values and planning derotational osteotomies. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective comparative study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large single-surgeon cohort (1,140 TKAs, mean 20.5-year follow-up) demonstrating combined coronal and rotational malalignment independently predicts aseptic revision, providing unique long-term alignment data.
bullets: CT-based tibial torsion measurements vary by up to 13 degrees depending on which proximal and distal reference axes are used, with all techniques differing significantly from one another.
These findings apply to any patient undergoing torsion assessment for rotational deformity workup, where the choice of measurement technique directly determines the numeric result.
Surgeons planning derotational osteotomies must confirm which technique generated the torsion value and compare it only against normative data from that same technique.

candidates.title: Functional outcomes over 24 months after arthroscopic repair of isolated subscapularis tendon tears in a multicentre study.
candidates.authors_short: Audigé L, Croci E, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Isolated subscapularis tears are rare, and it is currently unclear how the tear size relates to the postoperative outcomes after arthroscopic repair. This study aimed to evaluate clinical- and patient-reported outcomes, as well as adverse events of arthroscopically treated isolated subscapularis tears based on the tear extent over 24 months. METHODS: Across 19 orthopaedic centres, 69 patients undergoing primary arthroscopic repair for isolated subscapularis tears were prospectively recruited between June 2020 and November 2021. Medical imaging examinations were conducted at baseline and at 12 months. Clinical- and patient-reported outcomes were obtained at baseline, 6, 12, and 24 months. Adverse events within 24 months were documented. Patients were grouped into partial tears (n = 14), full-thickness tears of the superior half (n = 35) or complete full-thickness tears (n = 20) of the subscapularis. All outcomes were compared using generalised linear mixed models adjusted for baseline values, age, sex, American Society of Anaesthesiologists classification, tear aetiology, and steroid infiltrations. RESULTS: Improvements in all outcome scores were observed after surgery. No group differences were observed in the ranges of motion in flexion, abduction and external rotation (P≥0.634). The partial tear group had a higher pain level than both full-thickness groups at 12 months (P≤0.005). Abduction strength, Constant Score, Oxford Shoulder Score, Subjective Shoulder Value and EQ-5D-5L showed positive changes within 12- or 24-month follow-ups, with no group differences (P≥0.089). The risk of at least a symptomatic adverse event of any severity level affecting the operated shoulder and arm was highest for patients with partial tears (50%) and lowest for patients with complete full-thickness tears (25%). The most frequent occurrences were persistent or worsening pain, stiffness, and recurrent defects. Overall, 62% of patients with partial tears, 97% of patients with superior full-thickness tears and 77% of patients with complete full-thickness tears were satisfied at 24 months. CONCLUSION: Arthroscopic repair of isolated subscapularis tears leads to significant and sustained improvements in clinical and patient-reported outcomes over 24 months, regardless of tear extent. However, patients with partial tears demonstrated greater residual pain and fewer patients reported satisfaction compared with those with full-thickness tears. These findings may reflect differences in patient characteristics and surgical treatment choices. Further studies are needed to determine the suitability and efficacy of surgical treatments for isolated subscapularis partial tears. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, Retrospective Cohort Comparison, Prognosis Study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Registry-based cohort (1,683 shoulders) from the Dutch Arthroplasty Register evaluating glenohumeral radial mismatch and glenoid loosening risk, offering high-quality evidence on an important implant design parameter.
bullets: Arthroscopic repair of isolated subscapularis tears improves strength, range of motion, and patient-reported scores by 24 months regardless of whether the tear is partial or full-thickness.

Patients with partial subscapularis tears report more residual pain and lower satisfaction at 24 months compared to those with full-thickness tears, with only 62% satisfied versus 97% for superior full-thickness tears.
Surgeons should counsel patients with partial subscapularis tears that outcomes after repair are less predictable, and the role of surgery in this subgroup warrants further study.

candidates.title: 18-years Follow-up after Mosaicplasty in Adolescent Athletes with Osteochondritis Dissecans of the Elbow.
candidates.authors_short: Toftdahl L, Ovesen J, Thillemann TM
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty is an established surgical treatment of unstable osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) lesions of the elbow. However, the information on the long-term outcomes is lacking. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the long-term clinical and radiographic results after autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty in the treatment of OCD of the elbow. METHODS: This prospective long-term follow-up study is an extension of previously published data on 10 patients treated with autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty due to advanced, unstable OCD at the capitellum from 2003-2007. Objective and patient-reported outcomes were evaluated including Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), Oxford Elbow Score, Quick-Disability of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (Quick-DASH), Timmerman-Andrews Score, a Subjective Elbow Value, and Range of Motion (ROM). Radiographic signs of osteoarthritis were graded according to the Kellgren-Lawrence classification. RESULTS: At mean 18 years (range 16.0-19.7) five patients were available for follow-up. Mean age at follow-up was 34.4, and all five patients were women. MEPS was a median 100 (range 85-100). Activities of daily life were mildly affected in two patients. Two patients had non-symptomatic osteoarthritis grade 1 and 2. Patients experienced a functioning and near-normal elbow. CONCLUSION: The long-term results after mosaicplasty are encouraging, and we find it reasonable to recommend mosaicplasty as the surgical treatment in this group of female patients with advanced, unstable OCD lesions of the elbow. However, it is of concern that two out of five patients had non-symptomatic early radiographic signs of osteoarthritis at an early age. As this study has an inclusion rate of 50 % of the original cohort, attrition bias must be taken into consideration. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, case series, treatment study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Registry-based propensity-weighted cohort (1,415 rTSA) comparing cemented vs uncemented humeral stems for proximal humerus fracture, providing practice-relevant data on a rapidly evolving fixation debate.
bullets: At 18-year follow-up, adolescent athletes who had elbow mosaicplasty for unstable capitellum OCD reported near-normal elbow function with high patient-reported outcome scores.
Two of five patients developed early, asymptomatic radiographic osteoarthritis by their mid-thirties, suggesting ongoing joint monitoring is warranted after this procedure.
Mosaicplasty remains a reasonable surgical option for young female patients with advanced unstable elbow OCD, though the small follow-up cohort limits confidence in these conclusions.

candidates.title: Local Bone Density of Preoperative CT: A Predictor of Clinically Significant Shortening and Varus Collapse of Well-Reduced Geriatric Intertrochanteric Hip Fractures.
candidates.authors_short: Kashyap J, Kuhn MZ, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Intertrochanteric (IT) fractures are the most common geriatric hip fracture, with early fixation failure contributing to high morbidity and mortality. Lower bone density, as measured by Hounsfield units (HU) from CT scans, is predictive of various long bone fractures and fracture fixation failure, although its role in IT fractures is less well described. We aimed to assess the association between local bone density and radiographic outcomes after cephalomedullary nail (CMN) fixation of well-reduced geriatric IT fractures, hypothesizing that lower HU measurements are associated with increased rates of clinically significant shortening and varus collapse. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients older than 60 years with low-energy IT fractures treated with a long or short CMN between 2017 and 2024 at a single institution. Fractures with varus malreduction or tip apex distance >25 mm were excluded. Radiographs were assessed postoperatively and at 6 to 24-week follow-up to evaluate for shortening and change in the neck-shaft angle. Hounsfield unit measurements of the proximal femur were obtained from injury CT scans. Two-sample t-tests, simple linear regression, and multivariate logistic regression were used to analyze the relationship between HU and shortening/varus collapse. RESULTS: Among 103 patients (74 women, 29 men; mean age 79.3 ± 9.8 years), the mean local bone density was 193.3 ± 63.4 HU. Patients with clinically significant shortening or varus collapse (n = 38) had significantly lower HU than those without (n = 65) (160.9 vs. 212.3 HU, P < 0.0001). HU was independently associated with shortening/varus collapse (OR 0.98, P < 0.01) and negatively correlated with magnitude of shortening (R2 = 0.091, P < 0.01). An exploratory threshold of 150 HU significantly predicted shortening. CONCLUSIONS: Lower local bone density predicts shortening/varus collapse after CMN fixation of well-reduced geriatric IT fractures, despite optimization of modifiable surgical factors. An exploratory threshold of 150 HU may identify patients at risk of shortening within 24 weeks postoperatively.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large meta-analysis (N=10,853 imaging encounters) with pooled management-change rate of 0.02% after routine post-TJA radiographs, strongly supporting elimination of a costly universal practice.
bullets: In geriatric intertrochanteric fractures fixed with cephalomedullary nails, patients who developed shortening or varus collapse had meaningfully lower local bone density on CT scan than those who did not (161 HU vs. 212 HU).
A bone density threshold of 150 HU on preoperative CT identified patients at higher risk of construct failure within 24 weeks, even when reduction and implant position were optimized.

For older patients with intertrochanteric fractures, measuring Hounsfield units at the proximal femur on the injury CT can flag those who may need closer follow-up or augmentation strategies regardless of surgical technique.

candidates.title: Clinical Outcomes of Three-Dimensional Printed Implants in Bone Tumor Surgery: A Meta-Analysis.
candidates.authors_short: Qureshi S, Kralovich A, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The advent of three-dimensional (3D) printing has helped to revolutionize the field of orthopaedic surgery, particularly in the realm of preoperative planning and education. Another application of 3D printing in orthopaedic surgery is the production of patient-specific prostheses for reconstruction. The goal of this study was to analyze the use of 3D-printed prostheses in the setting of orthopaedic oncologic surgical resection and reconstruction. METHODS: A systematic meta-analysis was conducted using data from previous trials comparing 3D-printed prostheses (3DPs) with historical reconstruction across multiple anatomic locations, including the spine, pelvis, and extremities, in musculoskeletal oncology. Key outcomes assessed were surgical duration, intraoperative blood loss, complication rates, dislocation rates, resection accuracy, and functional outcomes using Musculoskeletal Tumor Society scores. RESULTS: A total of eight studies involving 237 patients (113 in the 3D-printed prosthesis group and 124 in the control group) were included. Compared with historical reconstruction, 3DP use showed a significant reduction in surgical duration (mean difference -37.6 minutes; 95% confidence interval [CI], -59.3 to -15.8; P = 0.0007) and postoperative complications (Odds Ratio [OR], 0.20; 95% CI, 0.07 to 0.59; P = 0.0038). The 3DP group also demonstrated significantly lower recurrence (OR, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.13 to 0.88; P = 0.026) and higher resection accuracy in the subset of studies reporting this outcome (OR, 14.36; 95% CI, 2.22 to 92.64; P = 0.0051). Functional outcomes improved with 3DP reconstruction, with a higher Musculoskeletal Tumor Society score (mean difference +3.78; 95% CI, 2.09 to 5.48; P < 0.001). CONCLUSION: Patient-specific 3D-printed protheses were associated with improved functional outcomes and favorable perioperative and oncologic end points, including shorter surgical time, fewer complications, and lower recurrence. These findings emphasize the value of 3DP technology in enhancing patient outcomes; however, owing to substantial heterogeneity and limited study volume, additional high-quality, randomized studies are needed to validate its broader clinical influence.
candidates.score_reasoning: Meta-analysis on hip fracture patients showing preoperative troponin elevation associated with 2.11x higher mortality risk, directly influencing perioperative risk stratification for one of orthopaedics' highest-volume patient populations.
bullets: In bone tumor surgery across the spine, pelvis, and extremities, patient-specific 3D-printed implants reduced operative time by roughly 38 minutes and cut complication rates by 80% compared with standard reconstruction.
Patients who received 3D-printed implants had lower local recurrence rates and higher resection accuracy, suggesting better margin control in musculoskeletal oncology cases.
Functional scores were meaningfully higher in the 3D-printed group, making these implants a clinically relevant option for orthopaedic oncology reconstruction when available.
